newsitem.title: USA: Perot says Clinton to face criminal charges.
newsitem.headline: Perot says Clinton to face criminal charges.

text.p: Reform Party presidential candidate Ross Perot said Monday President Clinton faces criminal charges that will bring on another Watergate-like constitutional crisis if he is re-elected.

Perot, in the final speech of his campaign, blasted away at Clinton for accepting campaign contributions from foreigners and refusing to say whether he plans to pardon former associates who have been jailed for convictions arising from the Whitewater political scandal.

"Our president, his wife and a number of his associates face serious criminal charges, some are already in prison," the Texas billionaire told a crowd of about 1,500 people at St. Mary's University in San Antonio.

"Would you allow a person with pending criminal charges to babysit your children? It's a joke," he said. "We are headed for a second Watergate, a constitutional crisis. With the financial problems our country has we don't have time for that."

Perot, who is trailing way behind in opinion polls for the presidential race, did not specify what charges he expected against Clinton. The president's personal and political finances have been investigated for the last two years by Whitewater special prosecutor Kenneth Starr, but there have been no indictments filed against Clinton or his wife.

At least three former Clinton associates have been convicted for illegal financial activities uncovered in the investigation, which arose from questions about the failed Whitewater real estate venture in which the president and first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton were investors.
Clinton has been mum on whether he would consider a pardon for his jailed former associates.

In recent weeks, he also has come under fire for allowing allegedly improper fundraising by the Democratic Party from Asian business interests. Clinton conceded no wrongdoing but called for campaign finance reform that included a ban on political contributions from foreign interests.

"I would urge you not to vote for a candidate who runs up and down the sidelines saying 'is it legal or illegal and if it is illegal what smooth things do I say to cover up and duck when I get caught,'" Perot said.

He also repeated his familiar themes about huge government debts and impending financial disaster if spending deficits are not trimmed. He said Clinton's claims to have led an economy that created millions of new jobs were misleading.
Perot was to close out his campaign Monday evening with infomercials on three national television networks.

Polls show Perot and running mate Pat Choate far behind Clinton and Republican challenger Bob Dole. Perot got a slight boost in recent days as campaign finance reform emerged as an election issue but he remained in single digits in most polls.
